description: Neon minds, chrome code, and data from the edge of the universe. We’re a Kyiv-based crew of netrunners building a game where anyone can design, launch, and run their own space mission, juggling budgets, power, and orbital physics along the way. Every choice matters. Every byte counts.
summary:
Space Owner is a game about flying to another planet with no way back. Your goal is to reach it, build a colony and stay. It is a mission that begins long before the rocket lifts off. The question is simple: what do you take when you cannot come back?

Every ship starts with the same basic kit: 23 tonnes of fuel, plus oxygen, water and food for 160 days and energy for 80 days. On top of that, you can load only 7 crates out of 12. You can take extra fuel, oxygen, supplies, a battery, solar panels, a reactor, a greenhouse, a regolith kit, an ice kit or a thermal kit. Five crates always stay on the ground, so you cannot have everything.

Then the flight begins. The game follows real physics, so nothing is scripted. Fuel, oxygen, food and power are used up as the ship moves. If you packed too little of something, the ship runs out of it and the mission ends before you arrive. If you chose wisely, you land, set up your colony and start a new life.

There is no single perfect loadout. More fuel means a longer trip, but less room for life support or a greenhouse. Every choice has a price, and every failure has a clear reason, so you can try again with a better plan.

Space Owner turns a hard topic into something you can feel. Instead of reading how difficult space missions are, you face the same trade-offs yourself. Every mission is different, and every landing feels earned. It runs in any browser, needs no installation and is made for curious players, students and classrooms.
details:
Space Owner - submission text

High-level summary

Space Owner is a game about flying to the Moon or Mars with no way back. Your goal is to get there, build a colony and stay. It is a mission that begins long before the rocket lifts off. The question is simple: what do you take when you cannot come back?

Every ship starts with the same basic kit: 23 tonnes of fuel, plus oxygen, water and food for 160 days and energy for 80 days. On top of that, you can load only 7 crates out of 12. You can take extra fuel, oxygen, supplies, a battery, solar panels, a reactor, a greenhouse, a regolith kit, an ice kit or a thermal kit. Five crates always stay on the ground, so you cannot have everything.

Then the flight begins. The ship flies past the Moon to Mars on a physical flight model: fuel, oxygen, food and power are used up as the ship moves. On the way the crew faces emergencies - a hull breach, a solar flare, a lost signal - and the cargo you packed decides which answers you have. If you packed too little of something, the ship runs out of it and the mission ends before you arrive. If you chose wisely, you land, set up your colony and start a new life.

There is no single perfect loadout. More fuel means a faster trip, but less room for life support or a greenhouse. Every choice has a price, and every failure has a clear reason, so you can try again with a better plan.

Space Owner turns a hard topic into something you can feel. Instead of reading how difficult space missions are, you face the same trade-offs yourself. It runs in any browser, needs no installation and is made for curious players, students and classrooms.

Project details

Space Owner is a browser-based space voyage simulation. The player prepares a one-way mission from the Earth past the Moon to Mars, and may found the colony on either of them. The ship always carries a base kit: 23 tonnes of fuel, plus oxygen, water and food for 160 days and energy for 80 days. On top of that, the player can load only 7 crates out of 12 available: three crates of fuel, oxygen, supplies, a battery, solar panels, a reactor, a greenhouse, a regolith kit, an ice kit and a thermal kit.

More than a third of the options must stay on the ground, so every choice is a trade-off. More fuel means more range, but less life support or power. A greenhouse or an ice kit may keep the future colony alive, but only if the ship gets there. The loadout decides how far the ship can fly. Pack wisely and you reach the destination, build a colony and do not return. Pack badly and the mission ends short of the goal. The voyage runs on a physical flight model, so resources are spent by physics; in-flight emergencies add risk that the right cargo can answer.

Benefits and intended impact

The game turns a hard-to-grasp topic into something you can try yourself. Instead of reading that spaceflight is limited by mass and resources, players feel it when their ship runs dry halfway. It works as interactive popular science: players learn why mission planning is difficult, why life support, power and fuel compete for the same limited space, and why colonizing another world is an engineering challenge before it is an adventure. It is free, needs no installation and runs in any modern browser, so it suits classrooms, science clubs and casual players. We want it to grow into a popular educational platform with more destinations, scenarios and real mission data.

Tools and technologies
The game is a browser application written in TypeScript on the Phaser 4 engine (WebGL, Arcade physics) and built with Vite. Code quality is kept by ESLint, Prettier and the TypeScript compiler. End-to-end smoke scenarios run the production build in headless Chromium. The flight model and voyage balance are checked by our own Node.js tools, which simulate whole voyages and verify the balance invariants. Location maps use the Tiled format and are generated by Python helper scripts. The music was composed in FL Studio. We used Git and GitHub for version control and ordinary personal computers for development; players need only a modern web browser.

The game is based on publicly available NASA data and resources: the orbits of the Earth, the Moon and Mars; NASA life-support figures for a crew member (oxygen, water and food per day); and the mission design resources of the challenge - Design and Develop Science Missions, the General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT), Concept Maturity Levels, the Mission Design Lab, NASA Mission Viz, A Learning Game About Telescopes and CubeSat 101. How each of them shaped the game is described in docs/NASA-RESOURCES.md in the repository.

Use of artificial intelligence

We used Claude (Anthropic) through Claude Code as an AI coding assistant. A large part of the source code, developer tools and technical documentation was generated or edited with AI assistance, then reviewed, tested and corrected by the team; AI also helped with the project descriptions. This is acknowledged in the repository README and in commit metadata (AI-assisted commits carry a Co-Authored-By: Claude line). The art, the music and the in-game texts were made by the team members without generative AI; the only exception is the short credits text of the About panel.

How it is creative

- One-way mission. Most space games are about going and coming back. Ours asks a harder question: what do you need to take if there is no return? The goal is to establish a colony.
- Planning is the gameplay. The game starts before launch. Choosing 7 crates out of 12 is the main decision, and the voyage is its consequence. There is no single perfect loadout, only trade-offs.
- Resources that depend on each other. Fuel, oxygen, energy and food are linked. A reactor, solar panels or a battery solve the power problem in different ways, and local-resource kits (regolith, ice) and a greenhouse reward players who think about life after landing.
- Physics first. Resources are spent by the flight model, not by a script, and the emergencies on the way can be answered with the cargo aboard. After a failure the scientists explain exactly why the ship fell short, so players can try again with a better plan.
- Learning without lectures. The science is built into the rules of the game, so players absorb it by playing.
- Tested balance. Our own tools simulate whole voyages automatically, so the game stays both realistic and fair.

Factors we considered

- Time. The hackathon timeframe was short, so we focused on one polished core loop (prepare, fly, colonize) instead of many half-finished features. Automated tests and AI-assisted development let us move fast without breaking things.
- Data and technology. The NASA data we had was enough for a credible model. We kept the browser game light by using Arcade physics, and put the precision into our own flight model, which is verified by separate simulation tools.
- Accessibility. No installation, no account, no special hardware. It runs on ordinary computers, in English and Ukrainian.
- Privacy and safety. The game collects no personal data and runs entirely in the browser.
- Scalability. Maps are generated by scripts in the Tiled format, and the crate system is easy to extend, so new destinations, scenarios and equipment are cheap to add.
- Scientific honesty and ethics. A one-way colony mission raises real questions about risk and responsibility. We present the game as an educational exploration of those challenges, and we simplify the science where needed without misrepresenting how spaceflight works.

Links
- Repository: https://github.com/vsevolod-ost/space-owner
- Play online: https://vsevolod-ost.github.io/space-owner/
